transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dina Chen (Redwood Solutions Architect), Rachel Kim (Pacific Data - Head of Cloud Security), Miguel Alvarez (Infra Lead), Priya Nair (Compliance)

Auto summary (auto-generated): Customer focused on encryption at rest/in transit, BYOK integration, HSM key lifecycle, and tenant isolation for a multi-tenant analytics platform. Action items and follow-up sandbox agreed.

Topics:
- BYOK + HSM connector design
- Tenant key lifecycle and rotation policies
- Key escrow, forensics, and emergency access
- Audit logs, traceability, and SOC 2/ISO controls mapping
- Data residency and network isolation for keys

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we have Pacific Data folks?
[00:00:12] Rachel (Pacific): Hey hi, Rachel here. Thanks, Alex.
[00:00:15] Miguel (Pacific): Miguel here. Priya's on as well.
[00:00:18] Priya (Pacific): Hello all.
[00:00:20] Alex: Great. Aim today is to walk through tenant-level key lifecycle and our BYO-HSM connector approach and make sure it fits your compliance needs, and figure out sandbox next steps. Samir will start with the architecture.
[00:00:35] Samir (Redwood SE): Cool. So at a high level, Redwood Private exposes a key management abstraction. For BYO-KMS we support two patterns: 1) HSM-backed envelope keys where the customer owns the root and we perform a key-wrap for model artifacts, and 2) tenant-specific KEKs stored in the customer KMS but referenced by our control plane.
[00:01:05] Rachel: Quick clarification — when you say "key-wrap for model artifacts" you mean model weights, token caches, and persistent KV cache?
[00:01:12] Samir: Right, model artifacts, persistent KV cache — sorry, KV cache sometimes gets transcribed as "KV cash" in our notes — and also any on-disk token caches. We don't keep plaintext model binaries in our multi-tenant store; they are wrapped with customer KEKs.
[00:01:30] Miguel: And how is the wrapping handled for per-tenant isolation? Do we have separate KEKs per tenant or a shared tenant root?
[00:01:38] Dina (Redwood): We recommend per-tenant KEKs for highest isolation. Practically we can support per-tenant KEKs in the customer KMS — each tenant has a unique key identifier. Redwood stores only the key reference and the wrapped blob.
[00:01:55] Priya: For SOC 2 and ISO 27001 controls we need proof of key separation. What audit evidence do you provide that tenant A's key wasn't used for tenant B's data?
[00:02:05] Samir: Our audit logs emit key usage events with key IDs, operation types (wrap/unwrap/rotate), timestamp, and the request route. We can export those logs to your SIEM or ship via syslog/S3 for retention. The logs include request ids and model artifact ids, but full request payloads are redacted.
[00:02:25] Rachel: Are those logs tamper-evident or signed? SOC auditors are pushing for immutable audit trails.
[00:02:31] Alex: Good question. We can push logs to an immutable store like an append-only S3 bucket with Object Lock or to your existing log ingestion that supports immutability. We can also provide a digest chain option where events are cryptographically hashed and the hash chain is kept for tamper detection. That's an advanced feature; Samir can run a demo in the sandbox.
[00:02:51] Miguel: Walk me through a typical key rotation. If a tenant rotates their KEK quarterly, how does that interplay with wrapped artifacts? Do you re-wrap everything or lazy re-wrap on access?
[00:03:03] Samir: We support lazy rewrap. On rotation, new encryptions use the new KEK, existing wrapped blobs remain accessible via the old KEK until used. We provide a bulk rewrap job that can re-encrypt objects proactively if required. That job can be scheduled during a maintenance window to control load.
[00:03:23] Priya: For our policy, we need proof of rewrap completion within 30 days if there's a suspected compromise. Can that be automated?
[00:03:30] Dina: Yes, we can run the bulk rewrap and provide a job completion report with counts of rewrapped objects and any failures. The report includes checksums and key id mappings for auditors.
[00:03:42] Rachel: About emergency access — backup keys, escrow — what's your stance? Some of our auditors want an escrow process with dual-control access in case of lost keys.
[00:03:52] Alex: Our recommended pattern is customer-managed escrow. We provide integrations and guidance for an escrow partner or a secondary HSM as an escrow. The customer controls the escrow policy. Redwood can store an encrypted copy of wrapped keys only if you opt in, with access gated by both Redwood logs and customer authorization. We avoid unilateral Redwood access to raw KEKs.
[00:04:15] Miguel: So Redwood will never have plaintext of the tenant master key?
[00:04:19] Samir: Correct. Under BYOK with HSM signing/wrapping, the plaintext root KEK remains in your HSM; Redwood only sees wrapped blobs and key references.
[00:04:27] [00:04:27] Rachel: OK that helps. Next — network and residency. We need HSMs to be in region us-west-2 and keys not to cross regions due to data residency. How do you ensure that?
[00:04:41] Samir: We support regional key binding. The HSM endpoint is configured per deployment and we route wrap/unwrap calls to the HSM's regional endpoint. The control plane also offers routing policies to ensure compute that handles unwrapping is in the same region or isolated in dedicated capacity.
[00:05:00] Priya: For the dedicated capacity option — if we want the lowest blast radius, can we run Dedicated in a VPC with a private link to our HSMs?
[00:05:08] Dina: Absolutely. Redwood Dedicated supports private connectivity via VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink. For on-prem HSMs we can use an SSH tunnel or a secure connector; we have customers doing HSM over TLS with mutual auth.
[00:05:21] Miguel: Quick note — we have a Thales pay shield and a cloud HSM for DR. Does Redwood have connectors for both?
[00:05:28] Samir: We support standard PKCS#11 and vendor-specific SDKs for most major HSMs including Thales and AWS CloudHSM. For pay shield specifics we may need a small connector shim; we'll validate compatibility in the sandbox.
[00:05:40] Rachel: Auditors also ask about separation of duties and RBAC for key ops. How granular is your RBAC around key usage?
[00:05:48] Alex: We have RBAC that maps to roles — admin, operator, auditor — and you can bind RBAC to SSO via SAML/SCIM. Key operations (create, wrap, unwrap, rotate, delete) are gated by specific permissions and we emit events for policy enforcement.
[00:06:04] Priya: Can we restrict unwrap operations so only dedicated infra nodes can call them, not the application plane?
[00:06:10] Samir: Yes. We support policy-based routing where unwrap calls for certain artifacts only occur on dedicated nodes with a specific fleet identity. Those fleet identities are themselves certified in your HSM ACLs.
[00:06:24] Rachel: What about encryption in transit — TLS sessions between Redwood nodes and the HSM? Is mutual TLS used?
[00:06:30] Samir: Mutual TLS for HSM connectors is the default. Additionally, we support client cert rotation and mTLS with pinned certs if your HSM requires.
[00:06:40] Miguel: Let's get into forensics — suppose we see anomalous decrypts, what artifacts can you provide?
[00:06:46] Dina: We can provide the unwrap event logs, request ids, IPs, node ids, and the key id. If you need packet-level captures or TLS session metadata, that can be captured if you run the HSM in your network and forward logs.
[00:07:00] Priya: Do you retain payload-level logs anywhere?
[00:07:03] Samir: No, Redwood does not retain plaintext request payloads. Only metadata and the wrapped blobs. We purposely avoid storing decrypted content to minimize blast radius and compliance surface.
[00:07:14] Rachel: On the topic of key verification, auditors ask for Key Check Values (KCVs). Do you compute and surface KCVs?
[00:07:20] Samir: We can surface KCVs as part of key import flows. The KCV can be recorded in the audit report. We also record the key thumbprint and key id.
[00:07:30] Miguel: About key import — we need strict import policies: customer generates key in on-prem HSM, then does an import to cloud HSM for DR. Does Redwood support split key import or multi-part import?
[00:07:40] Samir: Split/import flows depend on your HSM vendor. Redwood's connector is vendor-agnostic; we don't perform key imports ourselves but we can initiate or orchestrate import actions and validate KCVs. For split import, you'd use the vendor tools and we can validate the imported key via KCV and tag mapping.
[00:07:55] Rachel: Let's discuss retention and deletion. If a tenant requests full data deletion, how do we prove keys and wrapped blobs are destroyed?
[00:08:02] Dina: Deletion is multi-step: remove key material (in customer HSM or request rotate to a zeroized KEK), delete wrapped blobs from Redwood storage, and emit deletion audit evidence including object ids and checksums prior to deletion. We can provide a deletion certificate for auditors.
[00:08:18] Priya: Can deletion be irreversible? Some standards require cryptographic erasure — is zeroize supported?
[00:08:24] Samir: If the key is in your HSM you can zeroize the key which makes wrapped data unrecoverable. For on-cloud store, we can run secure delete policies and provide evidence, but for cryptographic best practice, zeroizing the root KEK in the HSM is the strongest mechanism.
[00:08:40] Rachel: Any limitations on per-tenant key count? We have thousands of tenants.
[00:08:45] Samir: We scale to large key counts; the limiting factor is HSM quota for keys. With AWS CloudHSM or Thales you'd plan quota. For very large fleets we recommend a hierarchical KEK strategy where tenant KEKs are derived or managed under a key family to reduce HSM objects while maintaining crypto separation.
[00:09:05] Miguel: Could you sketch that hierarchical model briefly?
[00:09:08] Samir: Sure — a master family key in the HSM generates tenant subkeys via a deterministic KDF or by wrapping ephemeral keys. The HSM still protects the master, but you avoid provisioning thousands of persistent HSM objects. We can show a diagram in the runbook.
[00:09:22] Alex: We should also note cost tradeoffs — HSM object count and wrap/unwrap QPS matter for cost. We'll include a sizing recommendation for your expected QPS.
[00:09:31] Rachel: Speaking of QPS, our analytics spikes can be high. Can you throttle per-tenant unwrap operations so noisy tenants don't affect others?
[00:09:39] Dina: Yes — there are rate-limiting and token-bucket controls at the tenant level and we can also do per-tenant circuit breakers that divert to cached plaintext in a private cache for short-lived tokens, but for security we prefer wrap/unwrap on demand with caching policies.
[00:09:55] Priya: Are those cache entries encrypted?
[00:09:58] Samir: Yes any cache at rest is encrypted with per-node ephemeral keys wrapped by the tenant KEK.
[00:10:06] Miguel: OK, hard topic: key compromise. Walk through the incident flow if a tenant KEK suspected compromised.
[00:10:12] Dina: Incident flow: 1) Customer notifies Redwood or Redwood detects anomalous unwraps, 2) Isolate tenant traffic by routing to dedicated nodes, 3) Rotate KEK and run bulk rewrap, 4) Push forensic logs and job reports to customer. We also support a temporary freeze mode where unwraps fail unless explicitly allowed by a dual-signed request.
[00:10:35] Rachel: Freeze mode sounds good. How is dual-sign enforced?
[00:10:38] Samir: It requires two distinct principals — e.g., an infra admin in your org and a Redwood operator — to sign a temporary unwrap waiver. Both signatures are recorded and immutable in the log. This is optional and typically used only for high-risk scenarios.
[00:10:56] Miguel: For the sandbox, what will you provision and what can we access?
[00:11:02] Samir: Sandbox plan: We'll spin up a Redwood Private instance in a customer-allocated VPC in us-west-2, connect to a test HSM instance you supply or an emulated HSM, configure per-tenant KEKs, and run rotation and bulk rewrap tests. We'll also enable audit log forwarding to your S3 test bucket.
[00:11:20] Rachel: Timebox? We want a 2-week sandbox and clear acceptance criteria.
[00:11:24] Alex: Two weeks is fine. Acceptance criteria proposal: ability to import a customer KEK into test HSM, perform wrap/unwrap flows for three tenants, demonstrate lazy rewrap and bulk rewrap, show audit logs with KCV and immutable export, and validate region binding.
[00:11:41] Priya: Also we want a deletion test and a compromise simulation.
[00:11:44] Dina: We'll include a simulated compromise run and a deletion pipeline.
[00:11:48] [00:11:48] Rachel: Great. Are there any compliance gaps you foresee for SOC 2 or ISO specifically?
[00:11:54] Samir: None major. The typical items we see are procedural — separation of duties, documented key access approvals, and backup/escrow policy. Technically we have the mechanisms; auditors will want to see policies and the runbook mapping to control objectives. We'll send a mapped control matrix.
[00:12:12] Miguel: Competitor question: we've looked at VaultCorp and CipherEdge. How is Redwood different on the key ops side?
[00:12:18] Alex: Two things: 1) Redwood's runtime is designed to minimize unwraps via KV/prefix caching for LLM workloads which reduces HSM pressure, and 2) we integrate the KMS/BYOK policy with routing and model serving so keys are first-class in deployment policies. We'll send a short comparative note.
[00:12:35] Priya: Ok let's go into a slightly nitty-gritty item — the key import flow UI. Who triggers and how are key owners verified?
[00:12:42] Samir: The UI has a key import wizard. Import requires an owner identity from SSO and an approval step (two approvals by default) before the key reference becomes usable. The wizard records KCV, owner, and time.
[00:12:57] Rachel: For auditors we need proof that owner approvals happened. Is that stored in the audit log?
[00:13:02] Dina: Yes, approval events are stored, signed, and can be exported.
[00:13:06] Miguel: A practical question — what credentials do we need to provide for the sandbox HSM?
[00:13:10] Samir: We'll need a test HSM endpoint, client certs for mutual TLS, and a service account with limited admin rights to create/import test KEKs. We'll provide a checklist.
[00:13:21] Rachel: Anything else?
[00:13:23] Alex: Let's surface a few edge cases — cross-tenant backup restores, multi-region rewrap, and large scale key rotations. We'll add these to the runbook and test one of them in the sandbox.
[00:13:36] Priya: I have one last requirement — our legal team insists on a clause that Redwood never performs emergency unwraps without documented customer consent except under court orders. Is that acceptable?
[00:13:46] Alex: Absolutely. We can include that in the contract and make the process auditable — no unilateral emergency unwrapping.
[00:13:54] Rachel: Good. Ok, let's capture next steps — who does what.
[00:13:58] Alex: Action items recap: Alex will send runbook and HSM connector diagram, Samir will provision the sandbox and run rewrap tests, Dina will prepare the control mapping for SOC 2/ISO, and Rachel will send compliance constraints and a sample policy.
[00:14:14] Miguel: Sounds good. Any open technical concerns?
[00:14:18] Priya: None from me.
[00:14:20] Rachel: No.
[00:14:22] Alex: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the sandbox kickoff. Thanks everybody.
[00:14:27] [00:14:27] (call wraps; remaining time used for side-bar Q&A and link sharing)
